cf.title: RLS bypass: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE/SELECT evaluates WHERE before RLS check

input.subject: RLS bypass: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE/SELECT evaluates WHERE before RLS check

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal or the reorder itself; the leak has a repro and the new order matches the CREATE POLICY docs. The one surviving objection, standards-compat-1, is fixable and concerns the backpatch through 14, which turns a silent no-op into an RLS error in minor releases and is untested on 14 and 15. That is a per-branch risk decision for a committer who knows RLS and the executor.

brief.title: Check RLS before the ON CONFLICT WHERE clause in DO UPDATE and DO SELECT
brief.problem: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and DO SELECT evaluate the user's WHERE clause on the existing row before checking that row against RLS policies. A user who cannot see a row can read its columns through a leaky function or use a plain predicate as an oracle. They only need to hit the row's unique key.
brief.proposed_design: The patch swaps the order in ExecOnConflictUpdate() and ExecOnConflictSelect() so the WCO_RLS_CONFLICT_CHECK runs before the ON CONFLICT WHERE qual. A row hidden by policy now raises the RLS error even when the WHERE clause would be false. The patch adds regression tests that use f_leak() in the WHERE clause of both paths.
user_visible_surface: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE and DO SELECT ... WHERE now raise the RLS error for a hidden conflicting row even when WHERE is false.
author_claims: The current order lets hidden column values leak through a WHERE function or act as a match oracle.
The CREATE POLICY docs say the existing row is checked against USING expressions first, so the fix matches the docs.
The DO UPDATE ordering dates from 168d5805e4 (2015); DO SELECT (88327092ff) copied it.
With the patch the repro no longer leaks and the regress suite passes.
The fix should be backpatched through 14.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible. A reviewer added himself in the CommitFest entry and removed himself the same day.
unclear: The author tested only master and 16beta2, but the commit asks for a backpatch through 14; behavior on 14 and 15 is untested.
The thread does not say whether the security team was told before the public post, or whether a CVE is planned.
The proposal does not say whether existing applications rely on a false WHERE skipping the RLS error, which the backpatch would change.
The thread does not discuss other places that run user quals before RLS checks, such as MERGE.

objections.title: Backpatch turns silent no-op upserts into RLS errors in minor releases
objections.failure_scenario: A multi-tenant application runs `insert ... on conflict (id) do update ... where <false for other tenants>` under RLS. Today, a conflict with another tenant's hidden row is a silent no-op. After a 14.x–17.x minor update, the same statement raises the RLS error, and the application finds out in production through failed transactions.
objections.argument: Message #1 and the commit message state the behavior change and ask for Backpatch-through: 14. The proposal does not say whether any applications depend on a false WHERE skipping the error, and minor releases normally avoid such changes. The author tested only master and 16beta2, and DO SELECT exists only on master, so the backpatch covers just DO UPDATE on 14 and 15, untested there. A committer would likely ask whether the oracle needs this change on stable branches, or whether master-only plus a release note is enough.
objections.author_must_show: Which existing upsert patterns would start erroring after a minor update, and why does the leak justify that change on 14 through 17 rather than master only?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 states the new error but does not weigh it for stable branches, and says 14 and 15 are untested. Security fixes often change behavior in minor releases, so this is a question to answer and stays fixable.

refuted.title: Backpatched order change turns silent no-op upserts into errors
refuted.failure_scenario: A multi-tenant application runs `insert ... on conflict (id) do update ... where t.tenant_id = excluded.tenant_id` under RLS. Today a key collision with another tenant's hidden row is a silent no-op. After a minor release from 14 onward, the same statement raises the RLS error and aborts the transaction.
refuted.argument: Message #1 states the behavior change, and the commit message asks for `Backpatch-through: 14`. The proposal does not consider applications that already depend on a false WHERE skipping hidden rows, and that pattern is a natural defensive habit in multi-tenant schemas. Matching the CREATE POLICY docs justifies the change on master. A committer would likely still ask whether stable branches need the same visible change, or whether there is a variant that closes the leak with less breakage.
refuted.author_must_show: Is the new error on stable branches the only way to close the leak, and how should a minor-release note tell users whose upserts start failing?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. It describes the same multi-tenant upsert that starts raising the RLS error after a minor update, and asks the same question about stable branches.

refuted.title: Backpatch to 14 changes upsert behavior in minor releases, untested there
refuted.failure_scenario: An application runs batched `insert ... on conflict do update ... where` as a role whose UPDATE policy hides some conflicting rows, and relies on a false WHERE to skip them. After a minor update on 14 or 15, those statements raise the RLS error and the batch aborts. The operator finds out in production, with no release-note warning in the proposal.
refuted.argument: Message #1 states that the patch changes behavior: a hidden row now errors even when WHERE is false. Yet the commit asks for `Backpatch-through: 14`, and the author tested only master and 16beta2. A committer would likely want this change justified per branch, tested on 14 and 15, and given a release note before it goes into stable releases. The fix for master looks low-cost and belongs in core.
refuted.author_must_show: Does the patch apply and pass on 14 and 15, and what release-note text tells users of a false WHERE that they may now see errors?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which already covers the behavior change in minor releases and the missing tests on 14 and 15.

Does the leak reproduce on 14 and 15, and does the DO UPDATE part of the patch apply and pass the regression tests there?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows row-level security enforcement and the ON CONFLICT code in nodeModifyTable.c, and who can judge behavior changes in stable branches. No committer has posted in the thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a new error in existing upserts on every branch that gets the fix, for the life of those branches, and for whether the fix closes the leak fully.
committability.author_follow_up: No sign either way; the thread has one message, though the author names the missing stable-branch tests himself.

priority.reason: The patch is 8.4 KB, touches one executor file plus rowsecurity tests, and fixes a leak for users who rely on RLS to hide rows. It has had no reply since 2026-10-06, and the backpatch decision needs a committer who knows the area.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so it is unchecked whether the reorder covers every path where the WHERE clause sees the existing row, or changes locking or EvalPlanQual behavior. The DO SELECT part exists only on master, so the stable-branch patch would differ.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow self-conflicting INSERT INTO .. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATEs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE accept a command whose own proposed rows conflict with each other, as DO NOTHING already does. Today such a command fails with "command cannot affect row a second time".
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Peter Geoghegan voted against it, and the CFM returned it citing those two votes. Andres Freund objected that the patch makes one command update a row it inserted, producing cmin == cmax and breaking heap visibility rules. The author then found visibility bugs in his own patch. Peter Geoghegan argued that updating the same row twice in one command is not desirable and asked who would want it.
matched_queries: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE WHERE policy
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: To me it seems as if allowing the same command to update the same row more than once is just not desirable in general.

precedents_retrieved.title: revamp row-security tracking
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the per-query tracking of whether row security applies with a global queue of row-security nest levels. get_row_security_policies() marks the levels, and higher-level callers such as fireRIRrules() read them, with cleanup after an ERROR.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed objected to the global variables, the hooks into transaction management, and setting the flag far from where RLS policies are applied. He proposed adding a hasRowSecurity output parameter to fireRIRrules() instead. The author wrote that design as v2 but worried it did not go far enough, and later planned to withdraw for lack of interest. Tom Lane replied that the topic needs more thought and suggested other designs, and the visible messages show no work after that.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm also not a fan of using global variables in this way, or the
resulting need to hook into the transaction management system to tidy
up. The end result is that the places where the flag is set are moved
further away from where RLS policies are applied, which IMO makes the
code much harder to follow.

precedents_retrieved.title: Row Level Security, leakproof-ness, and performance implications
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread started from slow queries under row-level security, caused by many built-in operator functions not being marked leakproof, and a patch marked enum_eq, enum_ne, textin and textout leakproof. Later proposals were a documentation patch listing RLS restrictions on the CREATE POLICY page, and Joe Conway's idea to redact error messages sent to clients plus a GUC to treat all functions as leakproof.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut wrote that redacting error messages had been found not to satisfy the leakproofness criteria, and Joe Conway accepted that the consensus was against him. Robert Haas suggested doing it outside core, with a logging hook and functions marked leakproof by hand, and doubted that customers could be supported with redacted messages. Peter also found the CREATE POLICY page the wrong place for the documentation patch and asked how a list of non-leakproof operators would be kept complete. The visible messages do not show which of these two patches this entry is.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think that approach has been found not to actually satisfy the leakproofness criteria.

precedents_retrieved.title: Document the limitations of row-level security
precedents_retrieved.summary: Pierre Ducroquet proposed a documentation patch, placed on the CREATE POLICY reference page, that lists performance-affecting restrictions of row-level security caused by built-in operator functions not being marked leakproof. The thread began with a patch that marks functions such as enum_eq/enum_ne and textin/textout leakproof and raised wider questions about leakproofness for array operators and functional indexes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut agreed that the leakproofness of built-in operators should be documented better, but said the CREATE POLICY reference page was the wrong place for it. He also said that such a list would be expected to be complete and maintained, while the patch covered only a few cases the author had found. He judged that the patch needed significant additional work and set it to returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Also, once you start such a list, there will be an expectation that it's
complete.  So that would need to be ensured.

precedents_retrieved.title: minor error message enhance: print RLS policy name when only one permissive policy exists
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the policy name to the row-level security violation error when exactly one permissive policy applies to an INSERT or UPDATE. The error then reads `new row violates row-level security policy "p1" for table "tts"` in place of the generic message.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed argued that a permissive policy grants access, so a failed check means no policy granted access, and naming the single policy as violated is inaccurate. He added that the patch only helps trivial one-policy cases, and suggested reporting the policy command type (for example SELECT) instead. Kirill Reshke set the entry to Waiting on Author because this objection was not addressed, and the visible messages show no reply from the author before the withdrawal.
matched_queries: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE WHERE policy
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So in the special case where there happens to be
exactly one permissive policy, it's not really accurate to say that
one policy was violated.

precedents_retrieved.title: conflict handling for COPY FROM
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andres Freund, Andrew Dunstan, Alvaro Herrera
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets COPY FROM skip rows that fail with unique or exclusion constraint violations, and later some format errors, up to an error limit set by a GUC or option. Failed rows go to a log file named in the command so the user can examine them.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that writing a server-side log file requires superuser rights, unlike COPY from STDIN. Andrew Dunstan and Andres suggested logging failed rows to a table or returning them as rows instead. Andres marked the entry returned with feedback after the author did not answer these comments for weeks. The author's later version reported skipped rows as warnings, which Alvaro Herrera called useless for this purpose; he supported returning rows.
matched_queries: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE WHERE policy
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Again, that requires super user permissions (in contrast to copy from/to stdin/out).

precedents_retrieved.title: Restrict EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) for RLS and security_barrier views
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch forbids EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) for statements that use row-level security or security_barrier views, so ordinary users cannot see how many rows the policy or view condition filtered out. Only members of a predefined role, proposed as pg_read_all_stats, could still run it in those cases.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed noted that the issue is not a security bug and that row counts can also be seen through pg_stat_get_tuples_returned(), pg_class.reltuples and plain EXPLAIN estimates, so EXPLAIN should stay as it is. After a discussion on pgsql-security, the author marked the patch rejected. The reason was that a determined attacker who can run arbitrary SQL can subvert row-level security anyway, so the restriction makes performance analysis harder without a real security gain.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Therefore, restricting EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) will do more harm than good, since it will make analyzing query performance harder without a real security gain.

precedents_retrieved.title: GUC to improve SECURITY INVOKER safety
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a boolean GUC, check_function_owner_trust, that raises an error when the session would execute a SECURITY INVOKER function owned by a role other than the current user or a role that can SET ROLE to the current user. SECURITY DEFINER functions would still run, so table owners could write triggers and similar code as SECURITY DEFINER for untrusted callers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund showed that SECURITY DEFINER does not protect a privileged user who runs code controlled by a less privileged user. Column default expressions and the default arguments of a SECURITY DEFINER function are evaluated with the invoker's privileges and can call functions in pg_catalog, so blocking only SECURITY INVOKER functions closes little. He proposed instead a setting that blocks any expression not controlled by a trusted user, plus an easy way to run statements under SECURITY_RESTRICTED_OPERATION. Jeff Davis accepted the examples, and the entry was withdrawn after that exchange.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: And I think my examples pretty conclusively show that security definer isn't a useful boundary to *reduce* privileges. So the whole idea of preventing only security invoker functions just seems non-viable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Allow ON CONFLICT .. DO NOTHING on a partitioned table."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Allow ON CONFLICT .. DO NOTHING on a partitioned table."
Reverted commit(s): Allow ON CONFLICT .. DO NOTHING on a partitioned table.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 8355a011a0124bdf7ccbada206a967d427039553, which
turns out to have been a misguided effort.  We can't really support
this in a partitioning hierarchy after all for exactly the reasons
stated in the documentation removed by that commit.  It's still
possible to use ON CONFLICT .. DO NOTHING (or for that matter ON
CONFLICT .. DO UPDATE) on individual partitions if desired, but
but to allow this on a partitioned table implies that we have some
way of evaluating uniqueness across the whole partitioning
hierarchy, which is false.

Shinoda Noriyoshi noticed that the old code was crashing (which we
could fix, though not in a nice way) and Amit Langote realized
that this was indicative of a fundamental problem with the commit
being reverted here.

precedents_retrieved.title: Track invalidation_reason in pg_replication_slots.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Track invalidation_reason in pg_replication_slots.
Reverted commit(s): Track conflict_reason in pg_replication_slots.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Till now, the reason for replication slot invalidation is not tracked
directly in pg_replication_slots. A recent commit 007693f2a3 added
'conflict_reason' to show the reasons for slot conflict/invalidation, but
only for logical slots.

This commit adds a new column 'invalidation_reason' to show invalidation
reasons for both physical and logical slots. And, this commit also turns
'conflict_reason' text column to 'conflicting' boolean column (effectively
reverting commit 007693f2a3). The 'conflicting' column is true for
invalidation reasons 'rows_removed' and 'wal_level_insufficient' because
those make the slot conflict with recovery. When 'conflicting' is true,
one can now look at the new 'invalidation_reason' column for the reason
for the logical slot's conflict with recovery.

The new 'invalidation_reason' column will also be useful to track other
invalidation reasons in the future commit.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P7] shares the RLS topic, but its recorded reason does not apply here. That reason was that a restriction which only hides row counts, already visible elsewhere, gives no real security gain. This proposal stops a leaky function in the ON CONFLICT WHERE clause from reading the column values of a row hidden by policy, which is a direct data leak. Message #1 points to no earlier discussion of this ordering, only to the commits that introduced it.
The new order matches the CREATE POLICY docs and adds no syntax, GUC, catalog or dump change, so the only compatibility concern is the backpatch.

The patch only changes the order of the RLS conflict check and the ON CONFLICT WHERE qual in the executor, so it adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, wire protocol or extension API state. The behavior change in a backpatch is a real question, but it belongs to another angle; the code was not shown, so possible struct changes could not be checked.

The leak is real. A leaky function and a plain predicate both see hidden column values, and putting the RLS check first closes both. The error that remains shows only that a conflicting key exists, which ON CONFLICT already shows. [P7] does not apply because that row-count issue was judged not to be a security bug. Two points are outside the design: the report was posted publicly instead of going to the security team first, and MERGE may need a separate check.

From a maintenance and fit angle the core change is small and adds no hot-path cost for non-RLS users, since it only reorders two existing checks. It also adds no new API. Regression tests pin the order for both paths. Precedent [P7] does not apply: leaky functions in quals are a threat that RLS is meant to stop.

No existing feature, option or extension closes this leak: the WHERE clause runs inside the executor before the RLS check, and users cannot change that order. The proposal changes the order and adds no new mechanism, so there is no duplication to object to. [P7] concerned a different problem (row counts in EXPLAIN ANALYZE), so its reason does not apply.

This is a security fix for a row-level security leak with a working repro. It does not add a feature, so the demand question does not apply. Everyone who relies on RLS policies to hide rows gains, and the visible cost is one ordering change that matches the documented behavior. [P7] differs: Dean Rasheed judged the EXPLAIN row counts there not a security bug, while here hidden column values reach arbitrary functions.
